 Model Information

 Description
 Gemini 4 Carbon is our model with frontier performance in long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, engineering, cybersecurity and scientific reasoning.

 Model dependencies
 Gemini 4 Carbon is based on Gemini 4 Argon.

 Inputs
 Text strings (e.g., a question, a prompt, document(s) to be summarized), images, audio, and video files, with a combined input-output token context window of up to 1M.

 Outputs
 Text, with up to a 1M token input + output.

For AI Studio and Gemini API, see the Gemini API Additional Terms of Service ; for Gemini for business and Vertex AI, see Google Cloud Platform Terms of Service . Access varies by channel and subscription tier (such as paid API tiers in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business, Google AI Ultra in consumer surfaces and Google Antigravity, and verified-defender access via the Fairwind Program ).  Additional benchmarks and details on approach, results and their methodologies can be found at: deepmind.google/models/evals-methodology/gemini-4-carbon .

 Intended Usage and Limitations

 Benefit and Intended Usage
 Gemini 4 Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence, such as complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more thinking tokens than Gemini 4 Argon to explore hypotheses thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops, with configurable thinking levels to balance quality, latency, and cost.
 It is particularly well-suited for applications that require:
 high-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis
 engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration
 strong visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail
 strong performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences
 cybersecurity defense, vulnerability discovery, and patching (with specialized capabilities available to verified defenders via the Fairwind Program )

 Known Limitations
 Gemini 4 Carbon may exhibit some of the general limitations of foundation models, such as hallucinations. In addition to this, we are continually working to improve jailbreak resistance and have recently strengthened the mitigations across Frontier Safety. There may also be occasional slowness or timeout issues, and at times the model may use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher thinking levels. The knowledge cutoff for Gemini 4 Carbon is March 2026, though in some domains the model’s knowledge may be less up to date. For more information about known limitations, see the Gemini 4 Argon model card .

 Acceptable Usage
 Gemini 4 Carbon is based on Gemini 4 Argon. For more information about the acceptable usage for Gemini 4 Carbon, see the Gemini 4 Argon model card .

The evaluation results are for automated evaluations and not human evaluation or red teaming. Scores are provided as an absolute percentage increase or decrease in performance compared to the indicated model, as described below.
 Overall, Gemini 4 Carbon outperforms Gemini 4 Argon across multilingual and multimodal content safety, while performing similarly on unjustified refusals and tone. We mark improvements in bolded green.

 We continue to improve our internal evaluations, including refining automated evaluations to reduce false positives and negatives, as well as update query sets to ensure balance and maintain a high standard of results. The performance results reported above are computed with improved evaluations and thus are not directly comparable with performance results found in previous Gemini model cards.
 We expect variation in our automated safety evaluations results, which is why we review flagged content to check for egregious or dangerous material. Our manual review confirmed losses were overwhelmingly either a) false positives or b) not egregious.

 Human Red Teaming Results
 We conduct manual red teaming by specialist teams who sit outside of the model development team. High-level findings are fed back to the model team. For child safety evaluations, Gemini 4 Carbon satisfied required launch thresholds, which were developed by expert teams to protect children online and meet Google’s commitments to child safety across our models and Google products. For content safety policies generally, including child safety, we saw similar or improved safety performance compared to Gemini 4 Argon. Additionally, the scope of red teaming covered potential issues outside of our strict policies, compared performance to Gemini 4 Argon, and found no egregious concerns.

 For more information about our frontier safety assessment, see the Gemini 4 Carbon Safety & Security Report .

 Safety and security were built into Gemini 4 Carbon throughout the training and deployment lifecycle, including pre-training data filtering, post-training alignment (supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning), product- and system-level safety filtering, and usage monitoring.  In this article 

 Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.
 Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.
 Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.
 To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.
 Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 

 1 
 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search .

 Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis
 Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.
 Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model.

 Using Google Antigravity’s new /swarm feature, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents turned historical photos and engineering plates into an interactive Three.js 3D exhibition of the Eiffel Tower's 1887–1889 construction from a single prompt.

 With seven public City Council planning PDFs (206 extracted engineering drawing views) and a single prompt, a multi-agent Carbon team using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature built an interactive 906K-triangle Three.js reconstruction of Google’s Platform 37 office across 10 overnight loops.

 In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Carbon built an interactive multiscale textile visualizer based on an academic paper, modeling a virtual-fiber finite element framework with interactive 3D yarn meshes, 110-fiber polar tracking, and dynamic stress-strain curves with minimal prompting.

 In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding.

 Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design
 Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.

 Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music. Try the live app .

 Paired with improved front end taste and motion design skills in Google Antigravity, Carbon reimagined the Google Merchandise Store in two prompts, proposing five art direction concepts and generating all-new product imagery with Nano Banana 2.1. Try the live app and Gemini front end design skill .

 Starting from a video reference generated with Gemini Omni in Google Antigravity, built a cinematic multi-shot underwater Atlantis scene. The pipeline modeled procedural ruins, volumetric caustic lighting, and water simulation in Blender before converting the full environment to Three.js for real-time browser rendering.

 Using a multi-agent loop in Google Antigravity, Carbon reconstructed a playable c. 1780 Stein-Schule fortepiano with 61-key escapement physics from CAD drawings and X-ray radiographs and placed it in a 3D model of the Royal Conservatory of Music's Koerner Hall in Toronto with seat-specific spatial acoustics. Try the live app .

 Frontier cybersecurity capabilities
 Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches.
 Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice.
 In Project Fortify , Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem.
 Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit . By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.
 As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies.

 Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning
 Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs.
 Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work:
 Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal . Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. items.content: # MiniMax-H3-Image-PE ## Online API Use MiniMax-H3-Image directly via API. - Global: [platform.minimax.io](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/guides/image-generation) | CN: [platform.minimax.cn](https://platform.minimax.cn/docs/guides/image-generation) API docs: - Text-to-image: [EN-docs](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-generations), [CN-docs](https://platform.minimax.cn/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-generations) - Image editing: [EN-docs](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-edits), [CN-docs](https://platform.minimax.cn/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-edits) - Prompt expansion: [EN-docs](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-context-ir), [CN-docs](https://platform.minimax.cn/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-context-ir) ## Introduction MiniMax-H3-Image-PE provides prompt expansion (PE) for [MiniMax-H3-Image](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image). It turns a short request into a detailed description of the intended image, together with an aspect-ratio recommendation for image generation. This repository covers two workflows: | Workflow | Input | Released assets | | --- | --- | --- | | **Text-to-image (T2I) PE** | A text instruction | MiniMax-H3-Image-PE weights (fine-tuned from [Qwen3.8-27B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), FP4), task and system prompts, and a client example | | **Image editing PE** | An editing instruction and reference images | A task prompt and message-assembly example for a vision-language model of your choice. **Image editing PE is still under development; this release provides its prompt only.** | The examples below explain how to use MiniMax-H3-Image-PE and the image editing task prompt. ## How to use T2I PE Run the examples from a local copy of this repository so the relative prompt and script paths resolve correctly. ### Serve MiniMax-H3-Image-PE We recommend SGLang with `sglang>=0.5.23` and `xgrammar>=0.2.7`. ```bash sglang serve \ --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image-PE \ --served-model-name MiniMax-H3-Image-PE \ --model-type llm \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --grammar-backend xgrammar \ --constrained-json-disable-any-whitespace \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 ``` SGLang reads the FP4 configuration from the checkpoint. XGrammar constrains the answer to the JSON schema, and the reasoning parser separates reasoning from the final answer. ### Expand a prompt Load the task prompt and insert your instruction with `.format(user_query)`: ```python from pathlib import Path task_prompt = Path("prompt/t2i/task_prompt.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8") user_query = "An orange tabby cat sleeping on a sunlit windowsill." user_prompt = task_prompt.format(user_query) ``` Send it with the system prompt and request parameters: ```python import json from urllib.request import Request, urlopen system_prompt = Path("prompt/t2i/system_prompt.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip() params = json.loads(Path("prompt/t2i/request_params.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")) payload = { **params, "model": "MiniMax-H3-Image-PE", "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}, {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt}, ], "stream": False, } request = Request( "http://0.0.0.0:30000/v1/chat/completions", data=json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8"), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, ) with urlopen(request, timeout=1200) as response: result = json.load(response) pe_result = json.loads(result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]) print(pe_result) ``` The included client performs the same request and checks the response: ```bash python3 scripts/expand_prompt.py \ --url http://0.0.0.0:30000 \ --model MiniMax-H3-Image-PE \ "An orange tabby cat sleeping on a sunlit windowsill." ``` ### Request parameters The examples load the defaults from [`prompt/t2i/request_params.json`](prompt/t2i/request_params.json): | Parameter | Value | | --- | --- | | `temperature` / `top_p` / `top_k` | 1.0 / 0.95 / 20 | | `min_p` | 0.0 | | `presence_penalty` / `repetition_penalty` | 0.0 / 1.0 | | `max_tokens` | 4096, including thinking and the final answer | | `reasoning_effort` | `xhigh` | | `enable_thinking` / `preserve_thinking` | `true` / `true` | | `response_format` | JSON schema for `expanded_caption` and `aspect_ratio` | ### Output With `--reasoning-parser qwen3`, `message.content` contains the JSON answer. Reasoning is returned separately in `message.reasoning_content`. Example output: ```json { "expanded_caption": "A warm photograph shows an orange tabby cat sleeping on a sunlit windowsill, with soft afternoon light falling across its fur.", "aspect_ratio": "3:2" } ``` When your aspect-ratio selection is `auto`, use the `aspect_ratio` returned by the model for image generation. If you select an explicit ratio, use your selected ratio instead of the model's recommendation at the image-generation stage. ## How to use Image editing PE Use the task prompt with a vision-language model that supports interleaved text and images. The example below describes message assembly without selecting a model or making an API call. ### Inputs Provide the following inputs: | Input | Description | | --- | --- | | `user_query` | The editing instruction. Refer to images in their supplied order. | | `references` | At least one prepared image, in order, with its original display aspect ratio as a reduced `W:H` string. Use `None` when the source ratio is unknown. | | `aspect_ratio` | The target ratio: `adaptive` to let the model choose, or an explicit positive-integer `W:H` string. | ### Assemble the message Load [`prompt/edit/task_prompt.txt`](prompt/edit/task_prompt.txt) unchanged as the first content part. Follow it with the image count, each image's label and source ratio immediately before that image, and your editing instruction and target ratio in the final text part. This produces one user message. The fixed task prompt forms a shared prefix across requests, allowing reuse by services that support prefix caching. Cache behavior depends on the provider. In the pseudocode below, `source_image` and `reference_image` are already prepared image inputs. The text and image parts are conceptual; adapt their representation to your model's interface. ```python import json from pathlib import Path task_prompt = Path("prompt/edit/task_prompt.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8") user_query = "Replace the bag in the first image with the bag in the second image." aspect_ratio = "adaptive" # Or an explicit ratio, such as "16:9". references = [ {"image": source_image, "aspect_ratio": "3:2"}, {"image": reference_image, "aspect_ratio": "1:1"}, ] count = len(references) content = [ {"type": "text", "text": task_prompt}, {"type": "text", "text": ( f"Reference Image Count:\n" f"{count} input image(s), labeled through ." )}, ] for index, reference in enumerate(references, start=1): metadata = "aspect_ratio unavailable" if reference["aspect_ratio"] is not None: metadata = f"aspect_ratio {reference['aspect_ratio']}" content.extend([ {"type": "text", "text": f"Reference Media:\n- [{metadata}]"}, {"type": "image", "image": reference["image"]}, ]) user_input = ( "\nUser Editing Instruction (JSON string):\n" f"{json.dumps(user_query, ensure_ascii=False)}\n\n" f"User Aspect Ratio Selection:\n{aspect_ratio}\n\n" "Apply the instructions above to the supplied inputs and reference images. " "Output only the required two-field JSON object." ) content.append({"type": "text", "text": user_input}) messages = [{"role": "user", "content": content}] ``` ### Output ```json { "expanded_caption": "", "target_aspect_ratio": "3:2" } ``` The description identifies source subjects, states what is preserved or changed, and describes new content. items.title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) built an agentic test orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that turns requirements into executable, governed tests for its Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients. Learn how specialized agents, per-tenant isolation, and workload-aware execution cut testing effort by 88% in an internal benchmark.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). 

 Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review.

 BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams.

 Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough

 TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow.

 TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting.

 To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients.

 Solution overview

 The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the platform across five stages, with a per-tenant security layer underneath. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront , with sign-in through Amazon Cognito . TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK . These agents generate the tests, refine them with the tester, and manage their execution. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) runs the generated tests. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon DynamoDB store the results, and Amazon CloudWatch captures the logs. Throughout, AWS WAF , Amazon Cognito, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and AWS Secrets Manager enforce per-tenant security and isolation.

 Figure 1: High-level solution architecture

 The TCS Agentic Test Orchestrator is a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) solution built on AWS. A tester provides requirements through Jira stories, business requirement documents (BRDs), Swagger specifications, uploaded documents, GitLab source folders, or captured UI flows. From those inputs the platform then generates test scenarios, Gherkin feature files, and executable Java or Python tests. It runs those tests on Amazon ECS, stores artifacts and results, and shows progress and reports in a per-tenant web application. The sections that follow describe how each part of the platform meets one of the four requirements TCS set.

 1. Separate the control plane from each tenant application plane

 TCS required strict isolation of each tenant’s identity, data, and keys, so the platform uses pooled compute with siloed data and identity. A shared control plane provides the Amazon EKS cluster, container registry, administrative portal, tenant registry, onboarding automation, Amazon CloudFront distributions, and AWS WAF protection. Each tenant application plane receives its own Kubernetes namespace, Amazon Cognito user pool, AWS KMS key, Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon DynamoDB tables, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases . This separation gives each BFSI tenant the data and key boundaries that financial-services controls demand.

 Tenant onboarding is event driven. The administrative API writes a pending tenant record, emits an event through Amazon EventBridge , and starts an AWS CodeBuild project that deploys the tenant infrastructure with AWS Cloud Development Kit ( AWS CDK ). This pattern makes tenant provisioning repeatable while retaining tenant-specific identity and data boundaries that TCS needed.

 2. Ground every agent in project context

 TCS’s first requirement was that generation reflect each project’s domain rather than a generic prompt, so grounding is built into the platform. The platform stores uploaded requirements and generated artifacts in Amazon S3 and session metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Project documents and synchronized source files are indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases using vector embeddings. Before material reaches an agent, retrieval is filtered by tenant, project, and session context, so one client’s context doesn’t inform another’s tests.

 This context layer supports the many ways a BFSI team expresses requirements: Jira stories and linked story chains, BRDs, Swagger definitions, reference code, locator documents, setup modules, test data, and GitLab source folders. For UI automation, a separate capture service uses Puppeteer to convert a URL and a natural-language goal into a UI flow document and an XPath locator document.

 3. Use specialized agents instead of one large prompt

 Because a single prompt can’t give a regulated workflow the control it needs, the platform divides the work among specialized agents that run as containerized services in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime using the Strands Agents SDK. A generation runtime routes requests to dedicated scenario, Gherkin, code-generation, and validation tools. Additional runtimes support conversational refinement, BRD-to-story conversion, incremental generation across linked Jira stories, and test execution. Each agent owns a stage of the lifecycle. Here’s a brief overview of each specialized agent:

 Generation agent: Creates structured scenarios, converts them to Gherkin, generates Java or Python automation, and validates generated code.

 Chat agent: Classifies a request as an information query or an update request, then answers or revises the active artifact.

 Dynamic task agent: Retrieves BRD context and produces a structured user story with requirements and acceptance criteria.

 Incremental agent: Extends scenarios, Gherkin, or code across a linked Jira story chain instead of starting from scratch.

 Execution agent: Fetches artifacts, chooses an execution environment, runs tests, classifies failures, applies controlled fixes, and saves final results.

 4. Route API and UI tests to the right execution environment

 TCS needed to cover both API and browser-based UI testing, which place different demands on infrastructure, so the execution agent detects the test type from the generated code and routes it accordingly. API tests are routed to Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate . Selenium UI tests are routed to an Amazon ECS cluster backed by Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) , where the executor can run Chrome with a virtual display.

 For UI runs, the executor can capture the virtual display with FFmpeg and publish an HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) stream to Amazon S3 for delivery through Amazon CloudFront. Test logs are sent to Amazon CloudWatch, and generated Cucumber reports are stored in Amazon S3 with time-limited access.

 5. Control the execution and correction loop

 To keep automated correction safe enough for a BFSI pipeline, the execution agent defines its fetch, execute, fix, and save steps as a LangGraph workflow. LangGraph’s explicit state graph gives TCS a fixed step order and a bounded retry loop, while AgentCore runtime hosts, scales, and isolates the agent that runs it. The fetch node retrieves the test project and generated assets, sanitizes files, and detects the framework. The execute node launches the selected ECS task, monitors status, retrieves logs, and parses results.

items.title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
items.summary: Running Amazon Bedrock across many accounts shows you the bill but not what happened inside each call. This post builds a centralized observability data lake that aggregates Bedrock invocation logs from every linked account into one queryable table, so you can see prompts, token counts, model choice, and per-invocation cost across your organization.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake

 If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call.

 You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s.

 We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it.

 What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today?

 Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch .

 The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you.

 What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake?

 A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization.

 Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts

 Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository .

 What does each Amazon Bedrock invocation log capture?

 After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table:

 The prompt the user or application sent.

 The model response that came back.

 Input and output token counts , so you can measure the true weight of each call.

 The model used, so you can understand utilization of models across teams.

 The stop reason (for example, max_tokens ), which tells you when a response was cut off.

 The account and timestamp , so you can attribute and time-slice everything.

 The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role , so you can see who sent the prompt.

 After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing.

 How is the Amazon Bedrock data lake designed?

 The data lake moves each invocation through five stages, from the moment Amazon Bedrock writes a log to the point you can query it in Athena.

 1. Amazon Bedrock writes an invocation log

 Every time an application calls an Amazon Bedrock model, Amazon Bedrock can record what happened: which model, which account, which IAM identity made the call, how many input and output tokens were used, and the prompt and response text. You turn this on once per account with a single API call, pointing Amazon Bedrock at a CloudWatch log group and giving it a role that can write there.

 2. CloudWatch forwards the logs to a central account

 Each source account gets a subscription filter on its Amazon Bedrock log group. Think of it as a permanent forwarding rule that says “send every new event to this address.” The address is an Amazon CloudWatch Logs destination living in your central account. Source accounts don’t get permissions on the central pipeline. They hand events to the destination, and the central account’s own role takes it from there.

 3. A small Lambda tidies each record

 CloudWatch doesn’t hand over clean JSON. It bundles events into batches and wraps them compressed and encoded, so what arrives looks like gibberish until you unwrap it. A small Lambda function does three jobs:

 Unwraps the batch back into individual log records.

 Throws out the noise. CloudWatch sends occasional housekeeping messages and plain-English notices like “Permissions are correctly set for Amazon Bedrock logs.” These aren’t invocation data, and letting them through breaks the next stage.

 Flattens one awkward field. The caller’s identity arrives nested one level down. The Lambda lifts it to the top so it’s straightforward to query later.

 4. Amazon Data Firehose converts to Parquet and writes to S3

 Amazon Data Firehose buffers the records and writes them to an Amazon S3 bucket, converting from JSON to Parquet on the way through. Firehose also files each object under a date path ( year=2026/month=08/day=27/ ).

 5. Use Athena to query the data and connect it to cost data

 An AWS Glue table tells Athena how to read those files, so you can query the lake with ordinary SQL. You can see which users are using the most tokens, which models are commonly selected, and what people are prompting. If you want, you can also connect this to the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) to get the spend of user prompts by day.

 What do you need before you start?

 A few things need to be in place before you deploy:

 AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials for each account.

 CloudFormation CAPABILITY_IAM and CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM permissions.

 At least one linked account (the account running your Amazon Bedrock workloads) and one central account to receive the replicated logs (these can be the same account).

 Python 3 with Boto3 ( pip install boto3 ), for the end-to-end test script.

 Cloned repo with all the resources in it.

 How do you deploy it?

 The order matters here. The central account stack has to exist before the linked account stacks can reference it.

 Stage 1: Deploy the central data lake stack

 Deploy the central CloudFormation stack first, into the account that will own the pipeline. Note two values from the stack outputs before moving on: the CloudWatch Logs destination ARN (which every source account needs) and the AWS Quick Sight role ARN (needed later if you deploy the dashboard).

 Stage 2: Deploy the logging stack in each source account

 Deploy the linked account CloudFormation. Repeat this for every account running Amazon Bedrock workloads. The source stack is small and takes a single input: the destination ARN from Stage 1.

 Stage 3: Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging

 Deploying the stack doesn’t start the logging. Amazon Bedrock logging is an account-level setting, not a CloudFormation resource. Activate it once per source account, pointing Amazon Bedrock at the log group and the logging role from Stage 2. Turn on CloudWatch delivery only.

 Stage 4: Verify data is arriving

 Run a test invocation in a source account, wait for Amazon Data Firehose to flush its buffer ( roughly a minute, sometimes longer ), then confirm Parquet objects have appeared under the data lake’s data/ prefix. Finally, check your S3 bucket to see data.

 Stage 5: Create the Athena view and query the data

 The central stack saves the view definition as a named Athena query but doesn’t run it. Execute that saved query once to create the flattened view. Run queries in the dedicated Athena workgroup, against either the raw table or the flattened view. The view is straightforward: token counts, cache tokens, stop reason, and prompt/response previews are already flat columns.

 How can you see costs of your Amazon Bedrock tokens?

 When you want a dollar figure against all of this, join the processed table to your CUR 2.0 data. The join key is the IAM ARN. You can use the following example queries in the Bedrock Data Lake SQL file.

 That one join turns the observability lake into cost attribution too: which prompts cost the most, cost per team or account by day, and what your least efficient invocations are actually costing you. It’s a great addition, but the data lake earns its keep well before you get there.

 What is tokenomics and why does this data lake matter for it?

 Tokenomics, the practice of managing the economics of artificial intelligence (AI) token consumption, was announced as a formal FinOps domain at the 2026 FinOps Foundation conference. It’s built on the same See, Save, Run, and Plan pillars as Cloud Financial Management, but applied to tokens instead of infrastructure. The challenge is that you can’t optimize what you can’t measure. Most organizations today lack the granular data needed to answer basic tokenomics questions: which teams are consuming the most tokens, and which prompts are wasteful. With per-invocation token and cost visibility, teams can match each workload to the model that fits it. That’s exactly what this data lake gives you. With per-invocation visibility into prompts, responses, token counts, models, and IAM identities, you have the foundation to start running a tokenomics practice rather than onl

items.content:
Machine learning 

 Mitra-v2: Scaling synthetic pretraining for tabular foundation models

 Expanding the mix of synthetic data used to train a tabular foundation model enables it to adapt to new tables without new models and lead the single-model field on the TabArena benchmark.

 By  Chris (Luyang) Kong 

 November 10, 2026

 5 min read

 Much of the data that businesses run on lives in tables: the rows might represent customers, transactions, or interactions, and their “attributes” are listed in the columns. Predicting missing attributes — such as likelihood of customer retention or how much demand to expect next week — is one of the most common machine learning tasks in industry.
 The standard tools for this job, such as gradient-boosted decision trees, produce models tailored to specific tables. Every new table means choosing an algorithm, engineering features, tuning hyperparameters, and setting up a processing pipeline. Tabular foundation models promise to end that cycle: one pretrained model reads the labeled rows of a previously unseen table and predicts the rest, with no training run in-between.
 Last year we introduced Mitra , a tabular foundation model pretrained entirely on synthetic tables. It worked well on small and mid-sized tables but ran out of room on large ones, wide ones, and problems with many classes.
 Today we're introducing Mitra-v2, the second generation of the model, for both classification and regression. We describe it in a technical report , and we've released versions fine-tuned for both classification and regression, along with the inference and fine-tuning code, under the Apache-2.0 license on Hugging Face. Amazon Connect Customer , which provides agentic-AI systems for core business functions, led the effort. Amazon Connect Customer is adopting Mitra-v2 for prediction on structured business and customer-experience data, such as estimating how likely a business-relevant event is to occur given a customer's interaction history and operational context.
 On TabArena , a public benchmark of 51 real-world datasets, Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field. It produces a better result than Mitra-v1 on 32 of the 33 datasets where both models run natively, and it completes all 51 datasets within the benchmark's one-hour budget, which Mitra-v1 failed to do on more than a third of them. On ScoringBench , a public benchmark for regression models that predict a range of likely outcomes rather than a single number, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 ranks first.
 A large language model is pretrained on huge volumes of data, so when you give it a few examples in a prompt, it can generalize from them with no additional training. Tabular foundation models work the same way. We pretrain Mitra-v2 on millions of synthetic prediction problems, and at deployment time the labeled rows of a real table serve as the examples. The model reads them and predicts the unlabeled rows, a technique called in-context learning.
 Every pretraining table is synthetic: we use no real data, and in particular, no customer data. The model learns general principles about how columns relate to one another rather than the contents of any real dataset. The lesson of the original Mitra was that the quality and diversity of those synthetic tables are central to how well the model generalizes.
 Mitra-v2 takes that lesson further. The architecture is unchanged: a Transformer that attends both across the rows of a table and across its columns . What has changed is the size of the examples the model sees during pretraining. Mitra-v2 is pretrained on tables with 10 times as many rows and roughly three times as many columns as those used to train Mitra-v1, so it has seen tables the size of the ones businesses actually use.
 We also added a new family of synthetic tables. To train the original Mitra, we generated tables from structural causal models (SCMs), which are graphs of cause-and-effect relationships between columns, and from tree-based models like the ones data scientists fit in practice. Mitra-v2's new hybrid SCM prior builds a single causal graph in which each relationship can be a small neural network, a decision tree, a smooth function drawn from a Gaussian process, or a time-dependent autoregressive process, so one synthetic table can carry the mix of relationships found in real tables. A new hybrid optimizer keeps training stable across this wider range.

 Overview of Mitra-v2. Top: the mixture of synthetic pretraining priors, with the classical structural causal model (SCM), gradient boosting, and forest generators alongside the new hybrid SCM prior, which composes neural, tree, Gaussian-process, and autoregressive mechanisms inside a single causal graph. Bottom: the scaled-up pretraining envelope, the two-dimensional attention backbone carried over from Mitra-v1, and the hybrid optimizer. 

 At deployment time, two lightweight wrappers extend the model beyond its pretraining limits. For very wide tables, we use singular-value decomposition to produce a new table that fits in the allotted space, populated with synthetic values that capture most of the variance in the original data. Mitra-v2’s output layer has only 10 nodes, corresponding to 10 classes, so for tasks with more classes than that, we send each node’s output toa a hierarchical tree, which further refines the classification.
 By default, Mitra-v2 is briefly, automatically fine-tuned on each new table it sees, producing eight copies whose predictions are averaged, a standard technique called bagging. So it isn't quite a zero-shot model. The adaptation adds some computational overhead, but in return, it delivers higher accuracy and gives customers additional options.
 We evaluated Mitra-v2 on TabArena, a living benchmark maintained by an independent academic team. TabArena ranks methods by Elo, the rating system used in chess, here computed from head-to-head wins across datasets under a fixed one-hour budget. Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field, as shown below, with large gains over Mitra-v1 on both classification and regression. It also ranks among the leading methods on the independent TALENT benchmark of roughly 300 datasets, where it's strongest on classification tasks with more than 10 classes. Full results, including per-dataset comparisons, are in the technical report.

 Elo ratings of Mitra-v2 and the leading tabular foundation models on the TabArena boards (top) and the TALENT boards (bottom), September 2026. 

 For regression, Mitra-v2 predicts a full range of likely values for each row rather than a single number, so users get prediction intervals along with the point estimate. That’s the approach that ScoringBench evaluates, rewarding forecasts that are both accurate and well calibrated. On the ScoringBench leaderboard, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 again ranks first.
 Mitra-v2 shows that a tabular foundation model can make substantial gains by widening the diversity and range of its synthetic pretraining, without a deeper network. We expect richer synthetic priors and adaptive mixtures to push this further. The fine-tuned classification and regression models and code are open on Hugging Face and ready to use, and we invite researchers and practitioners to try Mitra-v2 on their own tables.

items.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
items.summary: Our most capable vision-language-action model enhances robot dexterity, reliability, and safety
items.content:
November 10, 2026 Models 
 Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
 Carolina Parada

 Share

 Your browser does not support the video tag. 

 We’re enabling robots to learn faster for the real world - from everyday skills to the factory floor
 Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks.
 Earlier this year, we brought whole-body intelligence to robots of many types, including humanoids. Now, in large part thanks to Gemini 4 Argon's ability to accelerate robotics research, we have further pushed the frontier of physical intelligence. We tested Gemini Robotics 2.5’s capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity across over 200 distinct tasks, though this approach could scale to many more.
 Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks a leap forward in three key areas:
 Dexterity: Our robots can perform significantly more tasks with greater performance and dexterity — from using everyday tools to handling delicate, flexible objects.
 Reliability: During a real-world proof-of-concept on Mercedes-Benz production lines, our models helped Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid pick and pack automotive parts with a 96% success rate. This could enable robots to take on monotonous work, to enable technicians to focus on complex build tasks.
 Safety: As robots move into everyday environments, we have improved physical safety steerability and introduced a new benchmark to test against adversarial jailbreaks specific to robotics.
 Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to our robotics partners .

 Your browser does not support the video tag. 

 Your browser does not support the video tag. 

 Expanding task breadth, reliability, and dexterity
 Because real-world environments are unstructured and unpredictable, robots must be able to handle everyday objects with both fine precision and high reliability.
 With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks — such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.
 Our evaluations show significant increases in task precision, robustness, and speed. Compared to previous baselines, Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the type of task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster.
 Like our previous Gemini Robotics models, it natively works with many different robot types, including Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot (featuring the five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand) and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers.

 Slide 1 of 4

 Testing real-world reliability with Apptronik’s Apollo and Mercedes-Benz
 The ultimate measure of a robotics model is whether it can perform dependably in an active workplace. To put Gemini Robotics 2.5 to the test, we partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to use Apollo 2 humanoid robots on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany.
 Robots struggle to adapt to new unpredictable environments, our Gemini Robotics models give Apollo the ability to think, reason over multiple steps, and take action adapting to changes. In this proof-of-concept, Apollo 2 autonomously performs automotive kitting: the repetitive, physically taxing task of sorting individual parts from bulk bins into organized trays in the exact order needed for each vehicle on the line. Offloading this monotonous prep work helps keep the assembly line moving, while freeing up technicians to focus on complex build tasks.
 Using our embodied reasoning model ( Gemini Robotics ER ) to keep track of the workflow, and the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model to control its hands and arms, the robot reaches into supply bins, picks up metal automotive brackets, and places them into sequencing containers, all while correcting for any gaps. Achieving a 96% success rate, this pilot shows promising progress toward widespread real-world industrial applications.

 This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings. Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. This is the foundation for bringing humanoid robots to industrial and commercial environments at scale.
 Jeff Cardenas
 Co-founder and CEO, Apptronik

 Your browser does not support the video tag. 

 Apollo 2 using Gemini Robotics 2.5 to autonomously perform automotive kitting at a Mercedes-Benz factory.

 Advancing steerability and agentic safety for robots
 As robots operate in messy, everyday spaces, physical safety is paramount. To help ensure this, we have significantly advanced Gemini Robotics 2.5’s safety features.
 Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses inference-time reasoning guidance to steer around physical hazards in real-time. Much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Gemini’s responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%.
 We are also advancing safety for long-horizon, agentic tasks. Gemini 4 Argon currently leads our agentic robotics evaluations across unsafe task refusal, resolving uncertainty, and working in proximity to humans. To test jailbreak robustness, we are releasing ASIMOV-Jailbreak , a new open-source benchmark containing hundreds of prompts that disguise unsafe requests across dozens of scenes. Argon achieves a 99.5% jailbreak resistance — a significant improvement over the 82% rate of our previous baseline, Gemini Robotics ER 2.

 Your browser does not support the video tag. 

 Safe human-aware robot actions enabled by GR-2.5 steerability

 Accelerating robotics with Gemini 4 Argon
 To teach robots new skills, researchers need massive amounts of physical data and highly efficient modeling algorithms. Gemini 4 Argon’s robotics research capabilities helped solve these bottlenecks by acting as a simulation engine, which greatly accelerated our development of Gemini Robotics 2.5.

 Your browser does not support the video tag. 

 Examples of Gemini 4 Argon’s robotics research capabilities accelerating Gemini Robotics 2.5

 Argon can generate thousands of varied, simulated practice runs from a real-world camera scene and build a realistic digital twin. Combined with real training demonstrations, this enables the robot to more quickly generalize to new scenes and objects. Argon can also help researchers hypothesize why task failures happen from video footage and test the best improvements both in simulation and directly on real robots.
 Accelerated by frontier intelligence models like Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks an important milestone on the path toward solving physical AGI. By advancing in dexterity, real-world reliability, and rigorous safety, we are building the physical intelligence necessary for robots to work alongside people and solve real-world challenges

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.
items.content:
On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

 - Google Developers Blog

 On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

 NOV. 10, 2026

 Google AI Edge Team 

 Android ML Team 

 Share 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 LinkedIn 

 Mail 

 Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery . Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.
 This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:

 Android: faster, more accurate system speech models with ML Kit: Powered by Google’s latest on-device speech models, ML Kit delivers incredibly accurate multilingual transcription across 100+ languages at 10x real-time speed. It is paired with a few-step diffusion TTS model that begins speaking in just ~100 ms and synthesizes 24 kHz audio at up to 50x real-time speed. Both models are integrated into the OS, adding 0 MB to your APK.
 Web, Desktop and Beyond: cross-platform, open-weight speech with MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT: For cross-platform apps, we optimized new .litertlm model speech bundles, including Parakeet-TDT 0.6B, PocketTTS 100M, Kokoro-82M, and Phonon 31M. They deliver real-time streaming transcription and low-latency speech synthesis in a compact memory footprint, and run smoothly alongside on-device SLMs without compute contention.

 Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.
 Multimodal voice tutoring with XR Language Teacher
 Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?" , and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

 Link to Youtube Video 
 (visible only when JS is disabled)

 Seeing, speaking, and learning entirely on device 
 Live visual grounding and streaming voice input: Point your camera at a street sign, menu, or object and ask a question aloud. On-device ASR streams your spoken question in real time alongside the camera frame to Gemini Nano on Android devices —or Gemma 4 across other platforms—in a single pass.
 Structured outputs for bilingual TTS code-switching: Using a structured output schema, the model explains the scene in your own language while tagging foreign-language phrases separately, allowing the TTS pipeline to seamlessly switch voices and accents mid-sentence from your mother tongue to the target language alongside an on-screen vocabulary card.
 Adapt for intelligent eyewear 
 With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at Android Dev Summit: Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano . 
 Streaming voice dictation and read-aloud playback in AI Chat
 Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main AI Chat feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.

 Link to Youtube Video 
 (visible only when JS is disabled)

 Video of AI Chat Voice input + output

 Sentence-synchronized playback and configurable speech settings 
 ASR and TTS settings in Model Management: Choose between available ASR and TTS pipelines, preset voices, and downloaded language packs in one central place.
 Read-aloud playback with live sentence highlighting: Turn on “Auto-play TTS” or tap the speaker button on any response to launch a floating TTS bar that highlights each spoken sentence in real time, with the ability to jump to any sentence by tapping it.
 Reference implementation for chat voice outputs: Our open-source codebase demonstrates how to strip Markdown syntax, skip non-spoken blocks like code snippets and tables, and schedule synthesis at the sentence level to avoid compute and memory contention during LLM token generation.
 Under the Hood: Building with ML Kit, MediaPipe Tasks, and LiteRT
 While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our open-source code on GitHub shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using ML Kit , as well as MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform coverage and open model support.
 Building for flagship Android with ML Kit 
 For developers building for Android devices, ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through AICore and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.

 ML Kit GenAI Speech Recognition API : Streams live partial and final transcriptions as the user speaks, accepting audio from either the built-in device microphone or external audio streams such as smart glasses. Our latest on-device ASR advancements deliver incredibly accurate multilingual recognition across 100+ languages (reaching 8.0% to 9.0% Word Error Rate on FLEURS) while transcribing speech 10x faster than the real time audio being transcribed (~300 ms per 3 seconds of speech) and cutting end-to-end speech translation wait times by 35% to 44%.
 ML Kit GenAI Text-to-Speech API : Powered by a compact, few-step diffusion model accelerated on NPU, the on-device TTS begins speaking in ~100 ms and generates natural 24 kHz speech across 8 expressive voices and 21 locales at up to 50x real-time speed. It synthesizes a 27-second paragraph in just ~500 ms while cutting active device power by over 50% compared to traditional autoregressive TTS models, and includes built-in earcon support.

 Building across platforms with MediaPipe Tasks 
 Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines. MediaPipe Task simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:

 MediaPipe Speech Recognition (ASR) Task : Automatically handles audio framing, configurable Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and decoding. It supports real-time streaming, full-sentence batch, and hybrid transcription modes (streaming live words as the user speaks and refining the full sentence once speech ends), and showcases open-weight models like Parakeet-TDT 0.6B out of the box. Try it now directly in the browser!
 MediaPipe Text-to-Speech (TTS) Task : Provides a turnkey synthesis interface with voice selection and low-latency streaming audio output, showcasing open-weight models out of the box, including multilingual models like PocketTTS 100M and Kokoro-82M , as well as ultra-lightweight English models like Phonon 31M with sub-100ms Time-to-First-Audio (TTFA) on most devices and platforms. Try it now directly in the browser!

 Powering cross-platform speech and flexible model support with LiteRT 
 Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by LiteRT , Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.
 Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (multilingual ASR), PocketTTS 100M (multilingual TTS), Phonon 31M (ultra-lightweight English TTS), and Kokoro-82M (multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant Hugging Face LiteRT Community with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of multimodal model examples to help you get started, with more on the way.

items.summary:
Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. items.content:
By Jiarui Wang , Yuxin Cui , Bosen Ding , Zhaohui Guo , James Mason , Facundo Severi , Qingyuan Song , Ziyun Xu 

 Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. 

 We’re sharing how Your algorithm turns people’s natural language preferences into responsive recommendations, and how LLMs are tailored to specific tasks within the system. 

 Traditionally, the recommendation systems behind what people see on Facebook have learned from implicit engagement signals. While this allows them to scale well, it also means they adapt slowly and capture little nuance. But what if people could interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what they see to instantly make their recommendations more personal and customized? 

 Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations. This new suite of AI-powered tools lets people on Facebook state, in their own words, what they want to see in their Feed and Reels. By tasking a collection of large language models (LLMs) with understanding, storing, and tracking people’s stated preferences along with their user behavior, we’ve created a recommendation system that responds to people’s preferences and adjusts the content they see. 

 An Overview of the Your Algorithm System Architecture 

 The Your algorithm page has three parts (Figure 1):  

 At the top, a one-sentence Lately Summary that describes recent viewing activity.  

 Below it are two lists:  

 “Interested In,” prefilled with interests inferred from past activity.  

 “Not Interested In,” capturing topics the user has explicitly marked as not interested, or has X-ed out or hidden on Facebook.  

 People can use the interface to add interests (using natural language), move them between lists, or remove them. Every change applies responsively to both Feed and Reels, and will further update as the person gives feedback on individual posts.  

 Figure 1: The Your algorithm page. 
 Your algorithm system has several components that cover the full lifecycle of a preference, from inferring and validating it to applying it in ranking and delivery (Figure 2).  

 Profile generation builds the initial interest profile. 

 Preference management validates each change, enriches it with the signals ranking needs, and saves it to a single store that both Feed and Reels read, ensuring that the preferences shown on the page are the same ones used in ranking.  

 Ranking applies the “Interested In” and “Not Interested In” lists throughout the funnel.  

 Delivery optimization helps each change take effect more responsively. 

 Figure 2: An overview of the Your algorithm system. 
 From Preferences Into Recommendations 

 Turning a stated preference into recommendations poses three distinct problems. An interest added to Interested In needs to deliver relevant content quickly, without crowding out everything else. An interest added to Not Interested In needs to hold reliably, even though topics are fuzzy and any single filter misses some matches. And both need to take effect responsively, even when the next recommendations were cached before the change. 

 Your algorithm addresses each problem with dedicated logic across the recommendation funnel, from retrieval through reranking to the device (Figure 3). 

 Interested In: Surfacing New Interests Without Flooding 

 Each interest in Interested In drives four dedicated retrieval sources. Two find matching content directly (through search and through clusters of closely related topics), and two extend reach through the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Retrieving explicitly for each interest ensures enough relevant candidates for downstream ranking.  

 This is important because, without it, content about a brand-new interest might never enter the ranking pipeline at all. Candidates that pass a relevance check, which compares the meaning of the interest with each candidate, receive a promotion in late-stage ranking so they can compete alongside other content. A control layer in reranking then determines where they appear. 

 Responsiveness alone is not the goal. Our approach emphasizes balance over volume: A new interest should show up, not take over. The control layer spaces out recommendations for the same interest and caps each interest’s daily contribution. Retrieval also fetches candidates for only one interest per request, so every interest gets a turn. New interests receive extra weight for a limited period. After that, the recommendation system learns from how people engage with that content. 

 Not Interested In: Layered Filtering at Every Stage 

 Interests in Not Interested In are enforced at several stages based on different signals to achieve high precision and recall. During ranking, the same embedding-based comparison used in the relevance check removes candidates too close to an interest in Not Interested In, and demotion rules push down near matches. After ranking, the LLM reranker reviews the final list. On the device, cache invalidation, described below, removes matching candidates that are already queued for display. 

 Not every entry in Not Interested In is about a topic. Quality-related requests, such as reducing AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, map to dedicated demotion signals rather than topic matching. When a request names a creator, that creator’s content is filtered out directly. 

 Responsiveness Optimization 

 Even with ranking tuned to respond to preferences, there is still room to improve how responsively a change reaches what people see. Content for a new preference is not picked up until the next fetch request, and content already cached on the device was ranked before the preference was set.  

 We added two delivery mechanisms to close these gaps. When a new interest is added to Interested In, the system sends an extra fetch request outside the normal fetch cycle, called a supplementary tail load, to retrieve fresh recommendations so matching content appears quickly. When an interest is added to Not Interested In, cache invalidation handles candidates ranked before the change. The client obtains the new interest’s clusters and drops any cached content that matches them before it is displayed. 

 Figure 3: Where Your algorithm preferences act in the content ranking funnel. 
 LLMs Across the Preference Lifecycle: From Profile to Final Check 

 LLMs play a role at several key points in a preference’s life in Your algorithm. They generate the initial profile that people see on a first visit, validate each change as it is made, and give the final recommendations a last check against interests in Not Interested In (Figure 2). Each use comes with its own constraints, including latency, serving capacity, and safety, and evaluating them requires a new approach as well. 

 Profile generation provides the starting content for a first visit: the inferred interests and the Lately Summary. An LLM turns interest signals, which are refreshed regularly, into a set of inferred interests with clear, readable topic names. These are prefilled in the Interested In list and reflect past viewing across Facebook Feed and Reels. The LLM also writes the Lately Summary, a sentence that highlights ongoing interests. Together, they provide a recognizable starting point that is easy to review and correct. 

 Every edit on the Your algorithm page passes through preference management. When an interest is added or moved, an LLM checks that the phrase is a coherent topic, detects duplicates, and maps it to a clean topic name. This step runs on a smaller model that is efficient to serve at scale. The validated interest is then enriched with the signals ranking needs, such as an embedding and search keywords, and saved to the shared preference store. The LLM is only one layer of validation. The system also has a dedicated component that performs integrity and safety checks.  

 Once recommendations are ranked, LLM reranking provides a last check against interests in Not Interested In. The ranking funnel matches interests to candidates using embeddings, which are fast but coarse. To catch what they miss, a fine-tuned LLM reviews the ranked list and removes content it judges to be related to an interest recently added to Not Interested In. A key insight was that a small model fine-tuned to return only the items to remove was faster and more reliable than a general-purpose model judging each item individually. 

 Evaluating these LLM calls required its own approach. Standard offline metrics cannot tell whether a Lately Summary is accurate or whether the reranker removed the right candidates, so a separate LLM acts as a judge, grading each call’s output against expected behavior. This provides an objective, repeatable way to compare prompts and models before launch. 

 The Future of Your Algorithm 

 Your algorithm creates a more transparent and personalized recommendation experience, informed by both behavior and stated intent. But there are important opportunities remaining, such as better interpreting ambiguous input and making recommendations respond even more precisely to each request. We are also exploring additional entry points so that preferences can be shaped from more places. 

 Acknowledgments 

 This work reflects critical contributions from a cross-functional v-team across Meta (in alphabetical order): 

 Adi Gupta, Aryan Porwal, Bernabe Soto, Chao Yang, Chen Chen, Chen Kovacs, Chengxi Li, Chih-Wei Chang, Clare Yip, Cuong Nguyen, Dahni Ma, Daniel Thiyagu, Danny Kanoff, David Yuan, Devin Ding, Devon Pan, Eric Landgrebe, Feng Zhang, George Lu, Grace Yang, Hai-Son Dang, Haisen Hong, Hongyi Shi, Hongyi Wu, Howard Lu, Huijun Qian, Igor Vodov, Iordanis Fostiropoulos, Jakara Mato, Jasmine Neisser, Jason Liu, Jason Song, Jean-Pascal Billaud, Jeffrey Lin, Je
