items.content:
By Hongtao Yu , Peng Chen , Daohang Shi , Nick Riasanovsky , Lei Wang , Partha Kanuparthy 

 Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX) , is an extension to Triton that helps engineers optimize GPU performance while preserving Triton’s productive programming model.  

 TLX introduces explicit warp-group and cluster-level orchestration, letting developers adopt new hardware capabilities without sacrificing velocity.  

 TLX has demonstrated performance improvements in RecSys training, RecSys inference, and large-scale LLM pretraining. 

 Modern GPU architectures increasingly rely on execution-oriented features such as warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution to optimize their performance. But these same features also expose a growing gap between low-level programming models for control and high-level programming models for productivity. To bridge this gap, we built Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), an extension that gives engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton’s productive programming model.  

 Today, TLX powers production workloads across Meta, from AI training to large-scale LLM pretraining, enabling engineers to adopt new hardware capabilities quickly without sacrificing developer velocity. Across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, TLX is pushing the frontier of GPU performance — combining state-of-the-art kernels with explicit execution orchestration and model-aware fusion to deliver end-to-end improvements beyond what standalone libraries can achieve.  

 From AI Models to GPU Kernels 

 To understand where TLX fits, it helps to trace the path from an AI model to the GPU instructions that ultimately execute it. At Meta, machine learning (ML) workloads are built on a common software stack centered around PyTorch. Model code is transformed through graph capture, optimization, compilation, and lowering before eventually becoming GPU kernels running across large accelerator fleets. Over the past several years, Triton has evolved from an experimental kernel language into a foundational component of this stack. A significant share of production GPU kernels — both compiler-generated and hand-optimized — are now implemented in Triton. Improvements at this layer can therefore propagate broadly across training and inference workloads, making kernel performance an increasingly important lever for improving end-to-end system efficiency. 

 Figure 1: Normalized kernel count growth at Meta over a 10-month period (start = 1.0 in month 1). Over this period, Triton kernel count grew ~3.8x compared with ~2.0x for CUDA, reflecting Triton’s rapidly expanding role in Meta’s GPU software stack. 
 This shift has also changed who writes kernels. Kernel optimization is no longer the exclusive domain of GPU specialists. ML engineers routinely profile workloads, identify bottlenecks, and optimize the hottest kernels through autotuning, fusion, memory-layout improvements, or algorithmic restructuring. Triton’s productivity allows many of these iterations to happen in hours rather than days, enabling engineers to stay close to the model-development workflow. As a result, GPU kernel development has increasingly become part of the standard optimization toolkit for ML engineers. 

 Triton already provides a productive foundation for many memory-bound workloads through fusion and compiler-managed memory-access optimizations. Building on these strengths, TLX addresses a complementary challenge: coordinating execution groups, asynchronous data movement, and shared resources on modern GPUs. 

 The Problem: When Hardware Evolves Faster Than Programming Models 

 While Triton dramatically improved developer productivity, modern GPU architectures have evolved in ways that place increasing emphasis on execution orchestration rather than computation alone. NVIDIA’s Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPU expanded this trend further with Tensor Memory (TMEM), cluster-level execution, paired-CTA execution, and increasingly asynchronous execution mechanisms. These capabilities are not simply new instructions that can be hidden behind compiler optimizations, they fundamentally change how high-performance kernels are organized. 

 For example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.  

 As we adopted Hopper and Blackwell across Meta’s ML infrastructure, we repeatedly encountered the same challenge: CUDA could express these execution structures, but doing so often required large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code. Triton provided a dramatically more productive programming model, but many of the execution relationships required by modern hardware remained hidden behind compiler abstractions. 

 The result was a growing compiler catch-up problem. Each new hardware generation introduced new execution capabilities, while programmers either waited for compiler support to arrive or dropped into increasingly specialized implementations. We realized that the challenge was not simply missing compiler features, it was the absence of an appropriate programming abstraction. 

 The Missing Middle: Why SIMT and SIMB Weren’t Enough 

 The capabilities that matter most on recent GPUs operate neither at thread granularity nor at block granularity. Warp specialization partitions work across cooperating warp groups. TMA introduces dedicated agents for memory movement. TMEM enables new communication patterns between execution groups. Cluster execution lets multiple CTAs cooperate within a shared execution context. Organizing a kernel around these features means reasoning about how several execution agents cooperate, communicate, and synchronize — a level of structure that sits between CUDA and Triton. 

 This exposed what we came to view as a missing abstraction. CUDA’s SIMT model operates at too fine a granularity: It provides complete control, but requires developers to express every execution relationship manually. Triton’s blocked programming model operates at too coarse a granularity: It improves productivity, but turns many execution structures into implicit compiler decisions. Modern hardware increasingly requires something in between. 

 We refer to this model as Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW). MIMW elevates the warp group to the fundamental unit of orchestration. Rather than reasoning about individual threads or entire blocks, programmers express how multiple execution agents cooperate, communicate, synchronize, and share resources. This is the natural level at which many Hopper and Blackwell optimizations are expressed, and it is the abstraction layer TLX implements. 

 Figure 2 illustrates the evolution of GPU programming models. CUDA’s SIMT model exposed execution directly at thread granularity, giving developers complete control over scheduling, synchronization, and memory movement. Triton moved toward a SIMB model, raising the abstraction to blocked tensor computations and improving productivity. MIMW occupies the space between these two extremes. Rather than treating threads or tensor blocks as the primary execution abstraction, it elevates warp groups to first-class execution agents. 

 Figure 2: GPU architecture and execution model evolution. Recent NVIDIA GPUs evolved from mostly synchronous SIMT-style execution toward increasingly specialized and asynchronous execution, including Tensor Cores, Async Copy, TMA, WGMMA, TMEM, register reallocation, and paired-CTA MMA. This hardware evolution makes warp-group orchestration a programming-model concern rather than merely a compiler optimization. 
 The emergence of MIMW is not a software-design preference but a consequence of how hardware has evolved. Volta and Ampere exposed tensor cores through thread- and warp-level programming. Hopper made asynchronous data movement (enabled byTMA) and warp-group execution (enabled by WGMMA) central to high-performance kernels. Blackwell extends this trend further with TMEM, register reallocation, cluster execution, and paired-CTA MMA. Each generation pushes more cooperation across warp groups — and sometimes across CTAs — into territory that the programming model, not just the compiler, must address. 

 Figure 3: MIMW occupies the missing middle between SIMT’s fine-grained thread control and SIMB’s block-level productivity. TLX implements MIMW by adding explicit warp-group orchestration to Triton’s productive base. 
 Making MIMW practical requires expressing cooperating warp or wave groups as first-class execution tasks, with explicit control over shared-memory buffer access, synchronization, and handoff between them. TLX brings these capabilities into Triton’s existing tensor programming model, letting developers combine explicit execution control with familiar high-level tensor operations. 

 Introducing TLX: The Missing Middle, Implemented 

 We wanted  to avoid creating yet another standalone low-level language with TLX. Instead, TLX extends Triton with a second layer of execution-oriented constructs. Programmers continue to express computation using familiar Triton tensor operations, while TLX is used only where explicit control over execution, memory movement, or synchronization is required. In other words, Triton answers what computation should be performed, while TLX answers how that computation should be orchestrated. The difference is easiest to see through a simple tiled matrix multiplication. In standard Triton, execution follows a synchronous load-compute loop: Each tile is loaded, consumed, and then discarded before the next tile begins. 

 # Standard Triton: synchrono

items.content:
Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing.

 To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon , the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities.

 NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell , an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide.

 NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate , an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox.

 Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform : NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine , NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot . These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories.

 Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future.

 Securing AI Agents in the Open 

 NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards.  

 “The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. Bringing this work into the community enables broader collaboration on infrastructure that will be critical to the next generation of cloud-native applications.” 

 OpenShell gives organizations control over what AI agents can do. It applies deterministic controls to agent activity, so teams can enforce policies as agents use tools, access inference services and execute workloads. Its extensible architecture lets teams connect their own compute, inference providers, credential storage and monitoring tools. This allows organizations to apply governance across different deployment environments while integrating OpenShell with their existing enterprise systems. 

 Hundreds of organizations have put OpenShell to use, and the project has received tens of thousands of contributions in less than a year since launch.  

 Scaling Agent Execution on Kubernetes 

 Governing agents is only part of the challenge. Organizations also need to deploy them at scale. 

 NVIDIA is contributing to Agent Substrate, a Google -originated project in the CNCF Sandbox, and ensuring it works with NVIDIA Dynamo for model inference and KAI Scheduler for shared cluster resource allocation. This effort brings together agent execution, inference serving and resource scheduling on Kubernetes. 

 Agent Substrate preserves agent environments between tasks while releasing compute when agents are idle. By suspending and resuming those environments across a shared pool of agents, it lets teams scale agent workloads without keeping dedicated compute running for every session.  

 NVIDIA and Google are also collaborating on an integration of OpenShell and Agent Substrate, so enterprises can secure and govern agents across clouds and on-premises systems. 

 Building an Open Foundation for AI Factories 

 AI factories need to offer customers managed Kubernetes services while retaining control of their infrastructure, software and customer experience. Three new open source projects extend the DSX AI Factory Platform to make Kubernetes easier to run and inference faster to scale. 

 The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform software stack, from GPU infrastructure and Kubernetes management to workload orchestration and model serving. 
 NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) — now available in public preview — provide open source building blocks for delivering managed Kubernetes services on GPU infrastructure. They automate cluster lifecycle management and provide signed, version-pinned images. 

 NVKE and NVKR are launching with ecosystem support that extends their reach across AI infrastructure platforms and cloud services. Mirantis, Netris, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay , Spectro Cloud and vCluster, together with Firmus and SK Telecom , have aligned with NVIDIA on integration plans to bring NVKE and NVKR capabilities into their offerings. 

 NVIDIA Snapshot addresses the challenge of bringing additional inference capacity online quickly. Loading models and warming up workloads can delay scaling and recovery. The open source, modular component restores checkpointed replicas in seconds, without model reload or warmup, supporting faster startup, recovery and elasticity for inference and agentic workloads on Kubernetes.

 Autonomous vehicle (AV) developers need reasoning models that can operate within the compute and latency constraints of an onboard system. Larger models provide a foundation for developing these capabilities, but moving them into a vehicle requires additional work to reduce model size, preserve useful reasoning, and validate performance on the target hardware.

Built on the 2B Nemotron-based reasoning backbone of NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and paired with a diffusion action expert, it leverages surround-camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs to generate Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning and future driving trajectories. It reasons adaptively , generating reasoning only when needed, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving. 

 Alpamayo 2 Edge is post-trained with closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL) in NVIDIA AlpaGym , improving closed-loop driving performance by 48.9% on top of the best-performing checkpoint without closed-loop RL. Together, these capabilities give developers a strong, edge-ready foundation for bringing reasoning-based driving into an onboard stack.

 Making a reasoning model compact enough for onboard deployment introduces a key challenge: preserving the quality of its reasoning and driving behavior as model size is reduced. This requires a way to measure reasoning quality and use that feedback to improve the model. NVIDIA AlpaJudge is the human-calibrated evaluation and reward model used in Alpamayo 2 Edge development to evaluate reasoning traces, select higher-value training data, and provide RL rewards.

 Select training examples that expose useful learning opportunities

 Use human-aligned reasoning scores as rewards for post-training

 Together, these workflows connect an edge-oriented driving model with a repeatable process for measuring and improving it.

 Bring reasoning-based driving to the edge 

 An onboard driving model must interpret a changing scene and produce a useful trajectory within the system’s inference budget. The key question is how much driving and reasoning capability a model retains under that constraint.

 To balance model capacity and efficiency, Alpamayo 2 Edge leverages multiple new features:

 A 2B-parameter Nemotron-based reasoning backbone, sized for onboard inference

 Adaptive reasoning, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving

 Offline distillation, training with CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super

 Closed-loop reinforcement learning post-training in AlpaGym , in which the model learns from the consequences of its actions end-to-end in simulation

 Multi-resolution inputs to efficiently encode surround-view observations online

 Speculative decoding with DFlash2 to accelerate online reasoning without sacrificing quality

 AI-Generated Summary

 Agent Substrate multiplexes many agent sessions over a small pool of warm Kubernetes worker Pods, checkpointing idle sessions with full memory and filesystem state and restoring them onto any free worker.
 The runtime targets three workload types: coding assistants that alternate between LLM calls and repository operations, reinforcement learning post-training with bursty CPU-heavy environments, and short-lived GPU sandboxes for research compilation and benchmarking.
 Upstream contributions include request parking in the router to queue turns when all workers are busy, per-container resource limits for microVM sandboxes, and a vendor-neutral design for pausing and restoring GPU state using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation.
 NVIDIA Dynamo coordinates inference across GPU workers while Agent Substrate manages agent environments, with Dynamo's router using session identity, KV cache location, and tool-call boundaries to keep related model calls on workers that already hold reusable context.
 Dynamo exposes inference signals such as projected time to first token and GPU-pool saturation back to Agent Substrate, which uses them to decide whether to keep an actor resident, suspend it during long inference waits, or resume it as the model response nears completion.
 KAI Scheduler places the Substrate worker Pods alongside GPU trainers and inference servers, and the combined stack runs on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform with Substrate as an independent CNCF Sandbox project integrating with DSX OS components.

 AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per session holds memory for sessions that aren’t doing anything, and deleting Pods between turns pays a multi-second cold start every time and loses the agent’s state. RL post-training hits the same wall.

 Agent Substrate, now donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, is an open-source, security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. It multiplexes many sessions over a small pool of worker Pods. Idle sessions are checkpointed, memory and filesystem included, and restored onto whichever worker is free when the next request arrives. As agentic infrastructure fragments into proprietary runtimes that bypass Kubernetes, NVIDIA is contributing upstream to keep this work open.

 This post covers which workloads suit Agent Substrate, what is being built upstream, and how the project works with KAI Scheduler and NVIDIA Dynamo components in the DSX AI Factory Platform .

 The shape of an agent workload 

 Traditional web services run as a relatively small number of long-lived instances. Agents follow a different pattern: they wake up and take one step, running a shell command, editing a file, calling a test suite or calling an LLM. Then they wait, sometimes for milliseconds and sometimes for minutes, before the next step. The agent’s state (its filesystem, its processes, its working directory) has to continue between steps.

 Kubernetes struggles because spinning up a compute Pod for an agent means a trip through the API server, admission, etcd, the scheduler, the kubelet, image pulls and network setup. That takes seconds, which is fine for a service that runs for weeks. It’s far too slow for a sandbox that must appear, run a 10 ms bash command and get out of the way, hundreds of times per second.

 This leaves platform teams with two suboptimal choices: either keep one Pod warm per agent and pay for compute that is idle almost all the time, or create Pods on demand and pay a cold start penalty on every step.

 How Agent Substrate works 

 Agent Substrate uses Kubernetes for running a pool of ready pods. It creates a separate control plane that maps a large set of actors (agents and their environments) onto that smaller pool of workers. When an actor goes idle, it is snapshotted out of its sandbox (gVisor or a microVM) and its worker is freed. When the actor is called again, it is restored into whichever worker is free, with its memory and filesystem state intact. 

 Waking an actor doesn’t require a new trip through the API server, scheduler or kubelet. Agent Substrate restores the actor onto an existing worker instead. The worker pods are still ordinary Kubernetes Pods, so cluster scheduling, quotas and placement policies still apply as we describe later.

 The use cases driving demand 

 We see three kinds of workload driving demand for Agent Substrate:

 Coding assistants and agent serving: A coding agent alternates between LLM calls and work in its own environment: cloning a repository, editing files, running builds and tests. Users expect the environment to persist between turns and to respond immediately. A platform serving thousands of these sessions can’t afford a dedicated warm sandbox for each one.

 Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training with agentic environments: RL with verifiable rewards runs GPU trainers and generation servers alongside a fleet of CPU-heavy environments (code sandboxes, compilers, browsers, simulators) that execute actions and check results. Sandbox demand arrives in bursts as rollout batches dispatch actions. A training run can grow from a few hundred sandboxes in early experiments to many hundreds of thousands in production. The slowest environment determines when the trainer gets its next batch, so cold starts on that path leave GPUs idle.

 GPU sandboxes for research: A researcher’s coding agent needs a GPU, not to serve a model but to compile CUDA code, benchmark a kernel or run a numerical calculation. It launches a GPU sandbox on a shared cluster, runs the job and deletes the sandbox. Supporting this across an organization requires many short-lived, isolated GPU sandboxes that start quickly and share a limited pool of GPUs fairly.

 Upstream work: What’s landed and what’s next 

 Each contribution below started from one of those use cases. All of this work is public in the Agent Substrate repository :

 When every worker is busy, the next request waits instead of failing: In an oversubscribed system, such as a coding-assistant platform at peak or an RL rollout burst, a user’s next turn can arrive while every worker is busy. Agent Substrate used to return an error immediately, even though another actor would usually free a worker a moment later.

 Request parking in the Agent Substrate router ( #221 ) holds the request and retries the resume until a worker frees up, with a bounded wait and a cap on how many requests can wait at once. A follow-up ( #1229 ) makes sure requests to already-running actors never get stuck in that line.

 Giving agents a GPU inside their sandbox: The research GPU sandbox described above, along with GPU-backed RL environments such as simulators.

 We are working on device-pluggability that adds device support on Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Device vendors plug in their devices through a profile, each container in a sandbox requests only the devices it needs ( #752 ), and the same model works for both gVisor and microVM sandboxes. NVIDIA GPUs will be the first supported device.

 One container can’t starve or kill its neighbors: An agent sandbox often runs the agent’s workload next to helper containers for logging, proxying or metrics. Some of those may be untrusted. A runaway container shouldn’t consume the whole sandbox’s memory and take the agent down with it.

 Per-container CPU and memory limits for microVM sandboxes ( #859 ) addresses that issue. A container that exceeds its memory limit is stopped on its own, and the rest of the sandbox keeps running.

 Preserving GPU sandboxes across suspend and resume 

 When an agent pauses to wait for human review, its sandbox should release the GPU and resume later with its compiled artifacts and loaded data still in place. Supporting that requires saving and restoring both the agent’s state and the GPU state.

 Restoring GPU state introduces hardware compatibility constraints. A GPU checkpoint can usually be restored only onto the same GPU model, and sometimes only with the same driver version. Agent Substrate proposes a design to address this. 

 Device vendors describe how to pause their devices safely and which device properties a snapshot depends on. Agent Substrate records those properties with each snapshot and restores the sandbox on a matching device, or falls back to a clean cold start if none is available. The design is vendor-neutral and builds on DRA. NVIDIA GPUs are the first target; the design can be extended to other hardware types.

 NVIDIA Dynamo: Connecting the agent loop to the inference loop 

 Agent Substrate manages where agents act; inference runtimes manage where they think. Both face a similar efficiency challenge: keeping idle sandboxes warm wastes CPU and memory, while rebuilding model context on repeated model calls wastes GPU cycles.  NVIDIA Snapshot , a new open-source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , makes initialized GPU workloads reusable across inference replicas—speeding startup and recovery.

 When inference demand spikes or a replica fails, available GPUs don’t translate immediately into serving capacity. Initializing an LLM workload—a process known as a cold start—can take minutes, delaying scaling and recovery.

 Snapshot is a checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. It captures a fully initialized workload—including CPU and GPU memory—and restores that state on compatible infrastructure, bringing inference capacity online in seconds instead of minutes. Figure 1 shows the startup sequence. Snapshot skips repeated workload initialization; infrastructure provisioning and container image loading remain outside the measured restore path.

 Figure 1. Cold-start sequence: provision the machine, load the container image, start the inference engine, load model weights into GPU memory, compile with torch.compile, and capture NVIDIA CUDA graphs 

 This post explains how Snapshot checkpoints and restores GPU workloads, how platform teams can integrate it, and how restore times compare with cold starts across three inference engines.

 Snapshot for AI factory operations 

 Originally developed for NVIDIA Dynamo inference workers, Snapshot provides checkpoint and restore capabilities that other inference engines, schedulers, controllers, and platforms can integrate.

 Snapshot provides two operations for GPU Pods:

 Checkpoint : Once a workload is fully initialized, capture its CPU and GPU memory as a portable artifact.

 Restore : Start a new Pod from that artifact on any node with the same GPU model and driver. The process continues from where it was checkpointed, so weight loading, compilation, and graph capture are skipped.

 Both operations use Kubernetes custom resources. To checkpoint a Pod that is already running, create a PodSnapshot that names it. To start a Pod from a template and checkpoint it as soon as it is ready, create a SnapshotJob instead. To restore, add the annotation nvidia.com/restore-from to a new Pod, naming the PodSnapshot to restore from. The workload only needs a small handshake to pause before the checkpoint and resume after the restore. The repository has ready-made examples for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM .

 Snapshot can checkpoint and restore compatible workloads that span multiple GPUs on a single node as a single checkpoint artifact across ranks. This supports fast startup for large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models using parallelism strategies such as tensor parallelism (TP), data and expert parallelism (DEP), and decode context parallelism (DCP). Workloads must meet Snapshot’s checkpoint/restore and runtime compatibility requirements . See the example configurations .

 Benchmarks 

 Design partners have also evaluated Snapshot on their own workloads:

 Crusoe , an upstream contributor to Snapshot, reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness time from roughly 8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300.

 Saturn Cloud , a token factory platform, benchmarked NVIDIA Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference, cutting vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300 .

 The following benchmarks show how Snapshot accelerates inference startup across vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM)—with models from 600 million parameters to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with 1 TB checkpoints on 8 GPUs. Across all tested configurations, Snapshot brings a replica back in under 45 seconds, 8x to 36x faster than a cold start.

 Methodology 

 Each configuration was tested using two strategies on the same hardware and software stack:

 Cold start: The workload starts from scratch. The clock runs from process launch until engine initialization returns, before inference. The measurement is divided into four phases (Table 2):

 Startup: Starting the engine and worker processes, importing Python libraries, and setting up communication between GPUs. Some just-in-time (JIT) kernel compilation also happens here.

 Model load: Reading the model weights and constructing the model’s tensors, including any engine-specific conversion or repacking done while loading.

 Initialization: Preparing the loaded model to serve: memory profiling, allocating the key-value (KV) cache and runtime buffers, and other kernel and runtime preparation.

 Compilation, autotuning, and graph capture: Compiling kernels (for example, with torch.compile ), autotuning them for the GPU, and capturing CUDA graphs.

 Snapshot: The workload is restored from its checkpoint. The clock runs from the moment Snapshot is asked to restore until the workload is serving again. The measurement is divided into four stages (Table 3):

 Agent setup: The Snapshot agent on the node locates the checkpoint artifact and prepares the target Pod and GPUs.

 Checkpoint/Restore in Userspace (CRIU) restore: CRIU, the standard Linux tool for checkpointing processes, reads the process image from storage into host memory. Speed is set mostly by the storage backend.

 CUDA restore: Copying GPU state back into GPU memory.

 Wake/remap: Adapting the process to the new node and waking the engine.

 Both measurements exclude pulling the container image and setting up the container runtime. The KV cache release is triggered before every checkpoint, so it is not part of the artifact.

 Table 1 also reports checkpoint time and size: how long it takes to capture a fully initialized replica and how much storage the stored artifact requires. This is a one-time cost per model and configuration.

 The benchmarks show four main findings.

 Restore times stayed under 43 seconds: Across all tested configurations, Snapshot restored replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold start. The largest MoE models, with checkpoints of about 600 GB to 1 TB across eight GPUs, restored in under 43 seconds compared with cold-start times of 6 to 19 minutes.

 Restoring skips more than weight loading: Cold-start time includes loading weights, compiling and autotuning kernels, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot restores the initialized workload, skipping these repeated steps.

 Checkpointing pays off with the first restored replica: In every tested configuration, checkpoint time plus restore time was shorter than a single cold start. Checkpoint creation took 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes, depending on the model and configuration.

 Moving GPU state dominates large restores: For the eight-GPU MoE configurations, restoring GPU state took 18 to 29 seconds. Restoring CPU process state with CRIU took 4.2 to 10.8 seconds.

 NVIDIA is announcing two open source projects for building and operating managed Kubernetes services on GPU infrastructure—NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR). Both are new projects available in public preview.

 AI Factory customers often want to consume GPU capacity through the Kubernetes APIs, tools, and ecosystem they already use, with the factory operating their clusters. Delivering this service requires API-driven provisioning, tenant isolation, upgrades, and recovery, backed by service commitments. It also requires qualifying GPU hardware, networking, drivers, and runtime software across GPU generations and Kubernetes versions.

 NVKE and NVKR divide this work between cluster management and reproducible software builds. NVKE provides the software to run a managed Kubernetes service, installed on the factory’s infrastructure, with APIs to provision and manage clusters. NVKR builds the operating system images, container images, and packages those clusters need, using recipes that define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. AI Factories retain control of their software, operations, service, and customer experience. Teams can adopt NVKE and NVKR projects together or independently.

 Figure 1. The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform 

 Both NVKE and NVKR are components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , which helps AI factories design, build, and operate GPU infrastructure. Both projects are available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, so teams can inspect the code, develop in parallel, and contribute improvements. During the public preview, APIs, configuration, and behavior may change between releases. NVKE and NVKR are not yet recommended for production workloads. See preview status and known limitations .

 This walkthrough covers building a node image with NVKR, deploying the NVKE management plane, and provisioning a customer Kubernetes cluster.

 How NVKE and NVKR work together 

 NVKR builds the software: It produces node images, binaries, container images, and Helm charts from specific source versions and records the build inputs.

 NVKE manages the clusters: It uses those artifacts to provision and operate Kubernetes clusters.

 Teams can use the projects together or separately. NVKE has no runtime dependency on NVKR, and NVKR can build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems.

 nvkectl starts a temporary seed cluster on a bootstrap host and uses it to form a management cluster. The NVKE management plane, including the REST API and controllers, runs on the management cluster. The management plane creates workload clusters for AI factory customers, each with its own Kubernetes control plane, etcd, and node pools. Machines come from NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo) , which manages bare-metal lifecycle, through CAPNICo , the Cluster API infrastructure provider for NICo.

 A node must present an attested SPIFFE identity before it receives join credentials. The NVKE telemetry pipeline, an OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart, collects logs, metrics, and traces and exports them over OTLP to a monitoring backend.

 Figure 2. How NVKR, the NVKE management cluster, NICo, and workload clusters fit together 

 Inside each workload cluster, teams add the GPU-accelerated runtime with AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) , node packages with NodeWright , and break-fix automation with NVSentinel .

 NVKE is a Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer , conformance tested on Kubernetes 1.36.

 From bare metal to a customer cluster 

 This walkthrough describes how to provision a customer Kubernetes cluster starting from servers installed in a rack by building a node image with NVKR, deploying the NVKE management plane with nvkectl , and creating a customer cluster through the NVKE API. The NVKE documentation lists every flag and option, along with the most up-to-date steps.

 Walkthrough prerequisites:

 Three CPU servers for the management cluster, plus a separate Linux bootstrap host on the site network with containerd, nerdctl, kind, Helm, and kubectl

 Three CPU servers for the workload cluster control plane

 A pool of GPU servers for worker nodes

 A NICo installation with enrolled capacity

 A Linux build host with Docker and KVM support

 An HTTP server for the node image, a container registry for the controller image, and internet access to download the open source images and Helm charts used during installation

 Build the node image 

 NVKR defines the Kubernetes software configuration that NVIDIA validates for NVKE and provides the reproducible pipeline that turns that definition into deployable artifacts. NVKR builds node images from version-pinned sources and records every input, so teams can identify the software included in each image and can rebuild it later. The management cluster and each node pool can run different images, such as one per CPU architecture or GPU generation.

 Teams clone the NVKR repository on the build host. They then run the quickstart script to build nvkectl , the NVKE controller image, and its Helm chart, and a second script to build the node image, named node-image-01 in this walkthrough.

$ git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvkr.git && cd nvkr
$ bash scripts/nvkr-quickstart.sh
$ NVKE_OS_ARCH=amd64 scripts/nvke-os-local.sh node-image-01

 The node image build compiles the NVKE node agent and OVN-Kubernetes from source and adds checksum-pinned upstream releases of the Kubernetes 1.36 packages and the SPIRE agent. It then boots a virtual machine from the Ubuntu installer, installs the agents, and stages the Kubernetes and networking packages on the disk. The result is a QCOW2 disk image. Teams push the controller image to a registry, copy nvkectl to the bootstrap host, and put the QCOW2 on an HTTP server.

 Deploy the NVKE management plane 

 The NVKE management plane runs on a Kubernetes cluster called the management cluster. Teams run the following command on the bootstrap host to begin creating the management cluster:

$ nvkectl bootstrap site -f site-a.yaml \
 --nvke-controller-image registry.example.com/nvke/nvke-controller:<tag>

 The site specification file, site-a.yaml, includes the inputs that NICo needs to provision the three servers for the management cluster. The bootstrap command starts a temporary Kubernetes cluster on the bootstrap host. This temporary cluster uses kind to run a single Kubernetes node and hosts the NVKE software needed for the setup.

 The NVKE controller asks NICo for three servers, which NICo boots from the previously built node image. When all three nodes have joined, the bootstrap process deletes the temporary cluster, leaving the management cluster. Teams then install the NVKE management plane on the management cluster and run nvkectl config set-site to connect the command-line tool to the NVKE API.

 Publish a release set that customers will run 

 Customers choose a release by name from those that the AI factory publishes. They do not work directly with operating system images or cloud-init configuration.

 A release set has three components:

 A machine image holds the iPXE script NICo runs to boot a server.

 A cluster release pairs a machine image with the cloud-init configuration that prepares a control plane node and records the Kubernetes version that cloud-init installs.

 A node pool release provides the corresponding image and configuration for worker nodes.

$ nvkectl create machineimage -f machineimage.yaml
$ nvkectl create clusterrelease -f clusterrelease.yaml
$ nvkectl create nodepoolrelease -f nodepoolrelease.yaml

 Create a customer cluster 

 A customer cluster request includes the same NICo inputs as the site specification, plus a Kubernetes version. The control plane and each node pool have their own instance types, VPC prefix, and release. In this example, the control plane and GPU node pool reference releases named k8s-1
